newsitem.title: USA: U.S Treasuries little changed at midday after data.
newsitem.headline: U.S Treasuries little changed at midday after data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were little changed at midday on Friday, having reacted only mildly to several pieces of economic news.
A smaller-than-expected widening in the November U.S. trade deficit prompted economists to boost their estimates of fourth-quarter gross domestic product (GDP).

The Federal Reserve's data on November industrial production was also stronger than economists had anticipated. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond slipped about a quarter of a point on that news, but the retreat was short-lived.

Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust, said one reason the market staged only brief, mild reactions to the strong economic reports was that investors already know, and have discounted, a strong fourth quarter.

"The fourth quarter is going to be strong," said Feinman. "Everybody knows that. The market has backed up 40 or 50 basis points on that. More evidence of fourth-quarter growth will not move the market. It's a 'been there, done that' trade."
Feinman said two issues that are key ingredients of near-term Fed monetary policy remain unresolved.
"What matters is how much of the fourth-quarter momentum will move into the first half of the year," said Feinman. "And there's still no smoking gun on inflation."
"Therefore," said Feinman, "the Fed is not likely to move in February."
The market might see that scenario as altered if the fourth-quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI), due January 28, comes in strong, Feinman said.
"One percent or more on the ECI would be trouble for the market," said Feinman. "An eight-tenths of a percent rise would be ok. Something less than that would be good news."
Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi, said technicals also influenced trading.

"The level we were at after the bounce on Michigan sentiment was exactly where we were at a quarter to one on Thursday when Fed Governor Laurence Meyer's comments caused some selling," said Rupkey. "That level was 111-06 on the March T-bond contract which magically was the high in today's trading."
Rupkey said participants "are weighing what they want to do ahead of (Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan's (Congressional) testimony on Tuesday."

"Flows are both ways here," said Rupkey. "People are afraid of a warning from Greenspan on Tuesday, but at the same time, investors' ability to guess at what they key words will be out of a long testimony is Mission Impossible."

The market will close early at 1400 EST/1900 GMT today ahead of the three-day holiday weekend. The market will be closed on Monday in honor of the birthday of the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., the American civil rights leader.
In early afternoon trade, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was unchanged at 95-25/32, yielding 6.83 percent.
Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-19/32, yielding 5.97 percent. Five-year notes were up 3/32 to 99-7/32, yielding 6.31 percent. Ten-year notes were up 2/32 to 99-20/32, yielding 6.55 percent.
Three-month bill rates were down one basis point to 5.02 percent. Six-month rates were unchanged at 5.07 percent and year bill rates were down one basis point to 5.29 percent.
